strengths: Solid theoretical contribution with Theorem 5.1 providing an elegant explicit gradient for KLOT divergence that achieves 50-100× efficiency improvements over prior OT-based methods, eliminating practical memory bottlenecks

Thorough and convincing experimental validation with comprehensive ablations (Table 1), systematic robustness studies (number of pairs, unpaired samples, encoder choices), and careful baseline adaptations to the semi-supervised setting
Strong practical results demonstrating ~4× reduction in supervision vs baseline with consistent 5-7% gains on retrieval tasks, and robustness to cross-dataset distribution shift (Table 7)
Well-motivated semi-supervised alignment problem setting addressing practical scenarios where paired data is scarce but unimodal data is abundant
Insightful empirical support for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis showing that even simple linear alignment from 10k pairs achieves meaningful performance (~21-24% on COCO)
Reproducible work with clear Algorithm 1, extensive implementation details, single-GPU feasibility, and honest discussion of design choices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the two-stage framework combining a linear teacher with non-linear divergence-based refinement is relatively straightforward, with individual components (Procrustes, CCA, OT) being well-established techniques

Insufficient justification for KLOT choice: while Table 1 shows empirical superiority, the paper lacks rigorous explanation of why KLOT should preserve relational structure better than alternatives (CKA, InfoNCE); the choice of KL divergence in Eq. 12 is not theoretically motivated

Hyperparameter selection concerns: α is tuned on CC3M validation set but appears in training objective (Eq. 5), introducing subtle leakage for cross-dataset experiments; no sensitivity analysis provided for α or Sinkhorn parameters (n=100, ε values)

Baseline comparison fairness issues: S-CLIP was designed for domain adaptation (paired captions + unpaired images from same source) and its extension to cross-modal matching may not reflect optimal performance; semi-supervised SAIL variant unexpectedly underperforms but is not analyzed

Limited analysis of when/why semi-supervised learning helps: Figure 5 shows SSW distance explains only ~72% correlation with performance, leaving significant unexplained variance; no investigation of failure modes or theoretical characterization

Experimental gaps including no wall-clock time comparison with baselines, unclear computational requirements of 32k batch size, and saturation of gains beyond 500k unpaired samples limiting practical benefit

Narrow experimental scope limited to vision-language alignment; generalization to other modality pairs (audio-text, video-text) unexplored; all results use cosine similarity without exploring robustness to other metrics

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical scenarios with limited paired multimodal data and abundant unpaired data
Comprehensive experimental validation with consistent improvements across datasets, tasks, and encoder combinations; gains of +10.5% ImageNet and +5.5% COCO retrieval
Technical contribution: Theorem 5.1 provides explicit closed-form KLOT gradient eliminating memory bottlenecks (100× vs Sinkhorn unrolling, 50× vs implicit differentiation)
Simple yet effective two-stage design with linear teacher providing empirical support for Platonic Representation Hypothesis; systematic ablation of linear methods and divergences
Insightful distribution shift analysis quantifying relationship between unpaired data sources and performance via spherical sliced Wasserstein distance (r=-0.72 to -0.99)
Thorough experimental analysis including robustness across data sources, encoder combinations, and ablation studies examining paired sample count, unpaired data volume, and hyperparameter sensitivity
Clear presentation with detailed implementation details, reproducible results on single GPU, comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: linear alignment methods are well-established, two-stage pseudo-labeling is standard semi-supervised learning, and KLOT represents incremental extension of OT-CLIP and Van Assel et al. 2023 by allowing K*≠I

Modest gains from non-linear refinement layers (2-3% in many cases); linear teacher alone achieves 21-24% suggesting most benefits derive from unpaired data access (expected in semi-supervised settings)

Baseline comparison concerns: S-CLIP designed for different domain adaptation setting, STRUCTURE primarily supervised with semi-supervised adaptation potentially under-tuned, no comparison with semi-supervised methods from other domains

Missing theoretical analysis: no formal characterization of when semi-supervised alignment is possible, lack of sample complexity bounds or convergence guarantees, limited explanation of why unpaired data from different distributions helps beyond empirical correlation

Hyperparameter selection based on CC3M validation set not target test sets; different supervised/unsupervised ratios likely require different regularization weights α with limited practical guidance for selection
Setting specificity: results limited to frozen pretrained encoders with lightweight layers, primarily validated on vision-language alignment with unclear generalization to other modality pairs

KLOT divergence justification somewhat limited: Table 1 shows modest differences in some cases (Procrustes 30.0 vs 23.9 InfoNCE), relationship between ε and ε* parameters not thoroughly explored, intuition beyond empirical performance lacking

strengths: Solid technical contribution: Theorem 5.1 provides an elegant closed-form gradient for KLOT divergence, removing memory bottlenecks and achieving 50-100× efficiency gains over prior OT-based gradient methods. This result has potential impact beyond this work.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across multiple datasets (COCO, Flickr30k, SkyScript, LibriSpeech), tasks (retrieval, classification), and encoder pairs (DINOv2/v3, BERT, Qwen, NV-Embed), with consistent improvements of +3-10% in most settings.

Thorough robustness analysis: Systematic studies of robustness to variations in paired/unpaired samples, teacher noise, hyperparameter sensitivity (α, ε), and distribution shift. The mutual k-NN diagnostic (Pearson r=0.95) for encoder compatibility is a practical insight.

Well-motivated problem: Addresses the practical limitation that large-scale paired vision-language data are expensive to collect, especially in specialized domains. The semi-supervised setting is relevant and timely.
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with good motivation, helpful visualizations, detailed appendix with implementation details, and promise of code release.
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: The methodology combines existing ideas (linear teachers, pseudo-labeling, OT-based divergences from prior work like OT-CLIP and S-CLIP) in a relatively straightforward way. The main contribution is the KLOT gradient, which is solid but somewhat specialized.

Hyperparameter selection bias: The regularization weight α is selected based on CC3M validation performance but evaluated on different datasets (COCO, Flickr30k). Fair comparison requires selection on a held-out split from the same unpaired distribution to avoid favoring SOTAlign.

Unclear practical applicability and problem framing: The paper claims 'very few' paired samples are needed, but uses 10k pairs as default—still substantial for many specialized domains. Table 1 shows linear models achieve only 21-24% MeanR@1 with 10k pairs, and gains from unpaired data, while consistent, are modest (+3-10%). The '4× less supervision' claim (vs. 100k pairs) is not dramatic.

Lack of principled justification for KLOT: While Table 1 shows KLOT outperforms CKA and InfoNCE empirically, the paper provides limited insight into why. What properties make KLOT specifically better for semi-supervised alignment? How does KLOT leverage the 'shared structure' implied by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis?

Incomplete ablation studies: Limited analysis of which components matter most (linear teacher quality vs. KLOT divergence vs. nonlinear capacity). No clear ablation isolating contributions. Why do gains vary significantly across encoder pairs (3.8%-10.5%, Table 3)? If mutual k-NN predicts compatibility, should alignment efforts be selective?

Baseline adaptation concerns: The semi-supervised SAIL variant treats unpaired samples as negatives—not a standard semi-supervised approach. S-CLIP's pseudo-labeling is limited by the small paired pool. Other baselines (NNCLR, STRUCTURE) may not have been designed for this setting, potentially favoring SOTAlign.

No statistical significance testing: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported. Some gains are modest (26.5% vs. 21.0% on COCO T2I). Missing significance tests make it unclear if improvements are statistically meaningful.

Limited scope analysis: Assumes frozen encoders—performance with fine-tuning unclear. Batch size of 32k is large; scalability to smaller memory budgets not addressed. Only brief treatment of smaller models (ResNet-50, BERT). No comparison to SOTA foundation models or CLIP trained on billions of pairs—performance gap to state-of-the-art remains unclear.

Theory-practice gap for KLOT gradient: Theorem 5.1 shows efficient backprop, but the connection to improved alignment quality vs. computational savings is unclear. Figure 3 shows memory gains but not impact on final model quality.

Missing details and clarity: Some key details relegated to appendix. Sinkhorn hyperparameters (ε* = 0.005, ε/ε* = 10) are well-tuned for 100 iterations but generalizability unclear. Shared embedding dimension d=1024 chosen without justification. The two-stage approach could be motivated more intuitively upfront.

strengths: Sound theoretical contribution: Theorem 5.1 provides an explicit gradient formula for KLOT divergence with practical benefits (100× memory reduction vs. Sinkhorn unrolling, 50× vs. implicit differentiation)
Well-motivated problem addressing practical scenarios where paired image-text data are scarce (medical, scientific domains)
Comprehensive experimental validation with systematic ablations on number of paired/unpaired samples, multiple encoders, and linear alignment methods
Strong empirical results: +10.5% ImageNet, +5.5% COCO T2I, with gains up to +14% on specialized domains (SkyScript)
Insightful analysis of distribution shift quantification (Section 6.3) with Pearson r=-0.76 correlation between spherical sliced Wasserstein distance and performance
Practical diagnostic tool: mutual k-NN metric (r=0.95) for pre-screening encoder compatibility without training
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters in appendices, code availability promised, complete baseline implementations documented
Robustness demonstrated: graceful degradation under teacher noise (Table 8, r=0.5 corruption) and out-of-distribution unpaired data (Figure 11)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 2 pipeline diagram, Algorithm 1)
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily combines existing ideas (Platonic Representation Hypothesis from Huh et al. 2024, OT interpretation from Shi et al. 2024, semi-supervised alignment from Mo et al. 2023) with the main original contribution being Theorem 5.1, which is somewhat narrow in scope

Significant hyperparameter complexity: α ∈ {10⁻³, 10⁻⁴, 10⁻⁵}, ε/ε* ratio-dependent tuning (Figure 12), CCA regularization λ=0.1, Sinkhorn iterations—creates task-dependent hyperparameter selection without clear guidance for new domains

Variable and context-dependent improvements: gains range from +1% (Aircraft) to +10.5% (ImageNet); minimal improvements on CIFAR-10 (+1.3%) and Aircraft (+1.1%) are not explained; unclear when method excels
Incomplete mechanistic analysis: paper doesn't explain why CCA + KLOT (Table 1) reaches 30.3% MeanR@1 while supervised SAIL reaches only 24.2%—counterintuitive result lacks depth

Limited comparison with dedicated semi-supervised methods: SUE is the only existing semi-supervised baseline and restricted to single-dataset settings; most comparisons against supervised methods adapted to semi-supervised settings

Overstated validation of Platonic Representation Hypothesis: largely post-hoc validation via mutual k-NN correlation; doesn't address when/why PRH fails (e.g., ResNet-50 + BERT show minimal correlation)
Missing critical ablations: (1) no comparison of two-stage approach vs. end-to-end training with supervised + unsupervised losses; (2) necessity of linear teacher not empirically validated

Large gap to full supervision remains: SAIL with 1M pairs (35.5% ImageNet) substantially outperforms SOTAlign with 10k pairs + 1M unpaired (46.1%), but framing doesn't clearly discuss practical deployment scenarios and computational costs
Practical guidance under-discussed: no wall-clock time comparisons with baselines, limited discussion of encoder dependency, failure modes beyond noise injection not explored

Density of presentation: many design choices (3 linear methods, 3 divergences, multiple datasets) make core insights difficult to extract; hyperparameter selection strategies should be discussed upfront rather than post-hoc
